steps.html:
A boss who gives too much detail. A three-hour film. The ironing. Seven people describe the thing that bores them most, and none of them says the same as anybody else.

  • Follow seven short accounts and match them to their subjects
  • Use -ing as a subject, and the infinitive of purpose
  • Name emotions and reactions precisely
  • Write about what bores you and what you do about it

steps.title: Which sounds most natural?
steps.why: Bored with or bored by. And boring describes the thing, not the person feeling it.

steps.title: Study the words.
steps.sub: Sixteen items. Several are precise names for a feeling — the differences matter.

words.def: Feeling that nothing is interesting. Bored with or by something.
Annoyed and tired of a situation. Fed up with.
No longer willing to put up with something.
Showing no interest or energy about anything.
Not caring one way or the other.
Wanting something so much that you will do almost anything.
Not holding your attention. Neutral, where dull is a complaint.
To keep somebody interested and amused.
A strong feeling such as anger, joy or fear.
To relax after a period of effort or stress.
To stop paying attention and let your mind drift. Informal.
Your attention drifts away from what you should be thinking about.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: Three of the speakers begin with an -ing form: Listening to my boss… Watching a slow film… Doing the ironing…
steps.prompt: Why?
options: Because they are describing something happening now.
Because an -ing form can be the subject of a sentence, and that is what is being described.
Because they are answering a question that began with -ing.
steps.answer: Because an -ing form can be the subject of a sentence, and that is what is being described.
steps.why: Doing the ironing is the most boring job. The whole activity is the subject. That is this lesson's grammar.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: Three of the seven speakers describe being bored by having too little to do, not too much.
steps.prompt: What does that pattern suggest about boredom at work?
options: That most jobs are badly designed.
That boredom is not the absence of effort but the absence of anything worth directing it at.
That people who are bored are not working hard enough.
steps.answer: That boredom is not the absence of effort but the absence of anything worth directing it at.
steps.why: The seventh speaker finishes a task in five minutes and is bored again. The problem is not the workload.

steps.title: Where each form belongs
steps.html:
Not after a verb this time — in the other places English uses them.

-ing as the subject. An activity used as the subject of a sentence takes -ing: Doing the ironing is the most boring job. Never the infinitive at the front in everyday English: To do the ironing is… is possible but sounds archaic.

-ing after a preposition. Always, without exception: fed up with being stuck indoors, tired of doing the same thing, the point of it, instead of waiting.

The infinitive of purpose. To say why you do something, use to + infinitive: I put on music to unwind. Not for unwind, and not for to unwind. If you want for, it must take a noun: for relaxation.

The infinitive after an adjective. desperate to get off the plane, easy to understand, likely to happen, the first person to arrive.

too and enough both take the infinitive: too long to sit through, not interesting enough to keep me occupied. Note the word order: too + adjective, but adjective + enough.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the recording.

Listening to my boss.
An -ing form standing as the whole answer.

Watching a slow-moving film at the cinema.
Same again.

Doing the ironing is the most boring of all household jobs.
-ing as the subject.

That's a long time to be sitting in one place.
Infinitive after a noun phrase of measure.

I hate that feeling when you can't sit still.
Bare infinitive after can't.

I'm usually desperate to get off that plane.
Infinitive after an adjective.

I get really fed up with being stuck indoors.
-ing after the preposition with.

I feel a real need to get out and do something active.
Infinitive after a noun; the second to is dropped.

nothing more likely to send me to sleep than a dull lecture
Infinitive after an adjective.

doesn't give us an opportunity to discuss
Infinitive after a noun.

not having enough to keep me occupied
Enough + infinitive.

then you're back to doing nothing again
To is a preposition here, so -ing follows.

steps.title: The two kinds of ‘to’
steps.html:
1. Compare two sentences: I read to unwind. and I'm back to doing nothing.
  2. In the first, to introduces an infinitive and answers why: I read in order to unwind.
  3. In the second, to is a preposition, part of the phrase back to. Prepositions are always followed by -ing.
  4. The test: try replacing to with in order to. If it works, it is an infinitive. If it does not, it is a preposition and needs -ing.
  5. The phrases that catch people: look forward to, be used to, get round to, object to, back to. All prepositions. I look forward to hearing from you — never to hear.

steps.title: You are going to write about boredom.

options.label: The thing that bores you most
A time you were bored for days
What you do when your mind wanders

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least two -ing forms as subjects, at least two infinitives of purpose, and at least two adjective + infinitive patterns.
steps.html:
• Open with an <i>-ing</i> form as the subject.
  • Say what you have tried, and why, using infinitives of purpose.
  • Use an adjective + infinitive at least twice.
  • Close with what you now do, or fail to do.

Useful language

  • …-ing is, for me, the most boring …
  • I get really fed up with …-ing
  • By the end I'm desperate to …
  • I put music on to …
  • It isn't interesting enough to keep me …
  • Then you're back to …-ing again.
steps.modelHtml:
The forty minutes before a train

Waiting is the thing I am worst at. Not queuing, which at least moves, but sitting on a platform with forty minutes to go and nothing to do.

Reading does not work; I read the same paragraph six times. Walking up and down helps for about four minutes. By the end I am usually desperate to get on the train simply so that something has changed.

What I have started doing is bringing something small and difficult with me — a crossword, a page of a language book — specifically to fill that gap. It works, though I am aware that solving the problem this way is really just avoiding it.

Being bored is not fatal. But forty minutes is too long to spend doing nothing at all, and I have never once got used to it.
